speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON VISITS TO PARIS AND BONN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of the House may be interested in a brief report of my visits to Paris and Bonn in the past week. I went to Paris to open the new Canadian Cultural Centre there and to talk to Mr. Maurice Schumann, the French Foreign Minister, and to Bonn to return the visit paid to Canada last year by Mr. Willy Brandt, who is now the Chancellor, and to discuss matters of common interest with members of the German government.
Our new Cultural Centre in Paris will assist Canadians in France, especially students, and bring to the French people information about Canada, reflecting our bilingual and bicultural character and the many cultural strands that make up the Canadian fabric. The director of the centre is Mr. Guy Viau who was assistant director of the National Gallery here before taking up his new responsibilities. Mr. Viau is particularly well qualified for the job and I am sure that the centre, under his direction, will forge new ties between Canada and France.
The interest of the French government and the people in the new centre and in Canada as a meeting place of two great cultures was well expressed by the French government's representative at the inaugural ceremonies, Mr. Leo Hamon, who said:

What makes your country unique is the imbrication and the juxtaposition of its two cultures. This centre will fully reflect the originality and the wealth of resources of a country intent on retaining its own personality in the New World notwithstanding the size and power of its southern neighbour, which can be achieved only by preserving its diversity.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)

In Paris I met with the French Foreign Minister, Mr. Maurice Schumann. The principal subject we discussed was our bilateral relations, and the most important part for me was Mr. Schumann's categorical statement that the French government has absolutely no intention of intervening in the internal affairs of Canada. If there is no misunderstanding between us about this, and I hope there is not, our problems will be easier to deal with in the future.
I explained to Mr. Schumann what I consider to be the three basic elements on which good relations between France and Canada should rest: First, that co-operation between France and Quebec, which we regard as being of first importance, must be carried out in consultation with the Canadian government; second, that co-operation between France and Canada must be practical in nature and not confined to expressions of good will; third, that France must avoid taking positions contrary to the Canadian constitution.
As a result of this frank exchange I feel we have laid a foundation for avoiding in future some of the incidents which have in the past caused unnecessary strain and tension between us.
In Bonn my objective was to establish a better mutual understanding of our respective policies on international problems of common concern, and to prepare the way for more intensive bilateral co-operation between our two countries.
I got a first-hand account from the German Foreign Minister, Mr. Walter Scheel, of the federal government's efforts to improve relations with their eastern neighbours and to develop a more integrated community in western Europe, efforts which naturally form an overwhelming part of German preoccupations at the moment. I expressed the admiration of the Canadian government for the courage, imagination and realism of the federal government in these efforts.
The Germans expressed their appreciation for Canadian understanding and support. They also stressed the importance they attached to the maintenance of an active Canadian role in both the defence and detente
April 9, 1970

Minister's Visit to Paris and Bonn efforts of NATO. I reaffirmed the importance for Canada of our ties with Europe not only from the security point of view but also as a means of diversifying our external relations.
I discussed with several members of the German federal government ways of strengthening the functional co-operation between our two countries, particularly in the fields of science and technology, where both countries have something to contribute and something to gain from more intensive and systematic exchanges. We agreed to proceed in a pragmatic way to identify specific areas where the prospects for such exchanges are most promising. I hope it will be possible to send a mission to the German Federal Republic in the year to follow up these initiatives in greater detail.
I took the opportunity of these visits to let both the French and German governments know of the Canadian government's concerns about the repercussions of certain commercial and agricultural policies of the European Economic Community, particularly in relation to grain production and trade. Our desire is to increase consultations with the EEC on these matters so that the transatlantic co-operation to which we attach so much importance will be strengthened rather than weakened.

Mr. Speaker, we all welcome the minister back from his wanderings. I hope he will excuse me if I say I was given no previous notice of his intention to make a statement, nor do I have a copy of Sharp's Travels to assist me in my comments. However, after listening to him I can readily understand why that material might not be necessary.
We are happy that the minister visited France. Anything that can be done to improve relations between this country and France, and with the other European countries he visited, will be welcomed by us. No doubt we shall have an opportunity to comment further when we have examined the minister's statement in more detail.
The only further comment I would make is that it is probably unfortunate the minister did not remain here. He might have been helpful in preventing the action of the government and the Prime Minister in throwing away, by the introduction of bills and by other statements made yesterday, the legal works built up over a great many years by every Prime Minister from Laurier to the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson in establishing a claim to sovereignty over the Canadian Arctic. All of this was disposed of, notwithstanding

the legal phraseology and the petty quibbling of the Prime Minister and the government yesterday.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON VISITS TO PARIS AND BONN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this party are very glad to see the Secretary of State for External Affairs back in his place. We have listened with interest to his travelogue which might be described as "Innocence Abroad". We also listened with interest to the report he has given the House. Certainly all of us share the minister's hope that our relations with France will be greatly improved as a result of his visit and as a result of the better understanding that has been developing in recent months.
I was disappointed in press reports during the minister's visit which attributed to him statements that appeared to pour cold water on a full-fledged conference between the eastern and western powers as the government of Finland has been urging. The minister appeared to follow the line that no such conference would be valuable until all the i's were dotted and all the t's had been crossed. I think there are a great many Canadians and people throughout the world who feel that such a conference would be useful, that events are moving at such a rapid pace that any delay in the holding of such conference could prevent beneficial effects flowing from it.
The minister made no mention in his statement whether or not he had any discussions with the governments of France and Germany respecting the situation in Greece. There is increasing concern in Canada about the actions of the military dictatorship in Greece. Canadians feel that being associated with this dictatorship in NATO does not strengthen the hand either of NATO or of democratic countries. If the minister did have any discussions with respect to the attitude that the NATO countries are going to take to the military regime in Greece, I hope he will make a statement. If he did not have such discussions, I trust that discussions will be opened at the earliest possible date.
The minister also mentioned some discussions about the European Economic Community. I had hoped he would be able to tell us whether or not he was able to enter into any arrangements with the government of France respecting closer adherence to the International Grains Arrangement, since France is now one of the major exporters and also one of the countries that has been selling grain considerably below the floor in

I refer to a case which has been cited several times in the course of this debate, the case of Boucher v. The King, 1949-50. I am reading an excerpt from page 39 of the report of the Special Committee on Hate Propaganda in Canada. The last paragraph reads:
On this interpretation of the Boucher case, classes of Her Majesty's subjects may be adequately protected as groups, under the existing Canadian law of seditious libel, from violence or threats of violence against them, whether or not the violence is directed primarily against them. But on any interpretation the protection to groups extends only to situations where the prosecution can prove that violence was intended.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, no one can advocate genocide without advocating violence. Genocide is violence.
Elsewhere in the Criminal Code, for instance, among the seditious libel sections, provision is made for criminal actions to be brought against people who endanger the structure of our society by the incitement of hatred and violence. Bill C-3 would go further. It would seek-in my view, ineffectively-to silence the lunatic fringe without necessarily requiring evidence that their words were endangering the peace and good
April 9, 1970

order of the state. This, I maintain, is an attempt to use the criminal law to improve men's morals. I am not convinced that the criminal law can be effectively used in this way. I am not convinced that the law can be used to educate people. I am aware that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) does not agree. On Monday he told the House he feels the criminal law has a role as an educative force in Canada. I respect the Minister of Justice. I respect his integrity and his intelligence; I also respect his opinions. But in this case he and I have an honest difference of opinion.
Some of us were amused to hear the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) go into a peroration about dissension in the ranks of the government party which was going to drive the government out of office. What a high, faint cry that was from a defeated party anxiously grasping at any straw by which it might conceivably gain power. It is doubtful whether they would have a clear notion of what to do with power if they did get it. In the unlikely event that this bill is defeated, I would expect the government to promptly set down a motion of confidence; the hon. member for Calgary-North would then see very clearly where the members of the government party place their confidence and where they do not. But I disagree with the government on this piece of legislation.
In closing I should like to quote briefly from two articles on the subject. The first is part of a brief prepared by the British Columbia Civil Liberties Association. It is a very long brief but my quotation will not be extensive:
Reasonable though such suggestions may sound it should be remembered that while a politically free self-governing people can rightly authorize its governmental tribunals and agents to do many things in its name, including of course the prohibition of many acts deemed harmful, it can never rightly authorize its governmental tribunals and agents to serve as censor or screen for the citizens' minds. To authorize that, even in one area, thereby diminishes the people's self-governing capacity and renders them less fit for their civic role. Any such authorization, moreover, provides the principle and the precedent by which the procedure may be extended in order to suppress other expressions of hatred, not only "hate", ideas.
To the degree politically free people abdicate their sovereign, collective right to determine for themselves which ideas they shall hear or read,' which proposed policies they shall accept or reject, which doctrines they shall advocate or deny -to that degree they have hedged their democratic commitment, giving evidence thereby of a failure of nerve.
Hate Propaganda
I shall read, now, from another paper on this subject. This was contained in Chitty's Law Journal, Volume 18 No. 1. of January 1970 and the author is H. W. Arthurs, Assistant Dean of Law at Osgoode Hall. Incidentally, in his article Mr. Arthurs describes himself as a member of an identifiable minority group. He was speaking of the earlier bill; the bill has been amended since, but I doubt whether Mr. Arthurs opinions on it have changed. As appears on page 4, he says:
"If this bill is enacted, the general community reaction will be "now there is a law, and the business of combating hate propaganda is the job of policemen and magistrates". Not so. The job of combating hate propaganda is, and always must be, the job of every citizen. To enact a law is to invite the citizen to slough off his responsibilities, to hand over to his paid servants the moral burden which is his alone. I would prefer to see individual citizens -from the highest to the lowest-constantly confront and shout down the hatemonger and the bigot, rather than permit them to bask in the illusion that the forces of law and order, by prosecuting a few sad individuals, have obliterated prejudice.
In closing, I intend to say something which may surprise some hon. members. I should be delighted to find that my opinions with regard to this bill are wrong. I expect that the bill will pass. If it does, I devoutly hope that it will serve a worthy purpose by reducing the flow of hate literature in Canada and reducing the level of hatred in Canada, slight though it may be. But such is not my expectation and I shall therefore vote against this measure. I thank all hon. members for their attention.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, this bill has been the occasion for some speeches of a very high calibre on both sides of the subject. It has led to declarations of continuing faith in the democratic process and in the freedoms which are basic to that process. I have been particularly pleased, indeed, elated, by the fact that all hon. members who have spoken, whatever their side, have recognized the sincerity of all other hon. members and have contributed on the assumption that every one of us is as concerned about basic freedoms as is every other member. This attitude has led to the discussion of the merits of the enactment of this legislation free from the usual tangents which often affect us in debate.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I was therefore rather disappointed once or twice this afternoon when references of a

April 9, 1970
Hate Propaganda
political party character were made and accusations or innuendos expressed to the effect that the bill is before the House for political reasons-for the defence of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), of some other minister, or something of that sort.
I am in favour of the bill. I have expressed my support of it on a number of occasions, but because of the very attractive speech delivered by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) I beg the indulgence of members of the House to express once again my reasons for supporting the bill.
As a matter of fact, the right hon. member for Prince Albert himself gave us the reason the bill is of value. In defining what freedom means to him, he said-I think I am quoting him correctly, if not word for word-that "it means to me the right to be wrong and not to do wrong". May I say in passing that, like all of us in this House, the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert uses his right to be wrong quite often.
It is precisely because freedom means the right to be wrong, and not the right to do wrong, that it forms the basis, at least as far as I am concerned, of the bill that is now before the House. It draws a distinction between the two. A lot of words have been used in this House about attempting to legislate hatred out of people, to legislate evil out of people, and so on. No one has suggested the bill is designed to do that. Those who say that we who support this kind of legislation are thinking that the kingdom of heaven will be on earth the moment this legislation passes take us to be much more naive than we are.
No legislation will legislate evil or hatred out of the hearts and minds of those who have it. Indeed, I venture to suggest-I hope I do not sound too pessimistic-that so long as human organization continues to exist there will be prejudice, and that on occasion that prejudice will be turned into hatred in the hearts of some people. It is an historical and sociological fact that the majority in a society feels uncomfortable in the presence of a minority. It is an historical and sociological fact that a foreign element in a situation creates discomfort around it.
In every era in society there has been prejudice and hatred which has been based on religion, on colour, on race. I think it would be almost naively impertinent to think that we could ever eradicate the presence of prej-
udice and hatred by one group of another or by one person of another, and no one is attempting to do this.
What society has progressed in doing-and Canada is one of the best societies in this regard-is in persuading people in society, in legislating laws in society, which seek to limit the spread of both prejudice and hatred. This, in my opinion, is the very modest purpose that the bill seeks to serve. It does not seek to eradicate hatred or prejudice but seeks, both through the executive power of the law and through the educative power of the law, to limit to some extent the spread of hatred and prejudice.
No one in this House has greater regard for the civil liberties fences erected by the right hon. member for Prince Albert. But I say to him that his definition of freedom and the kind of-I was going to say self-righteous but perhaps that would be unfair to him-the kind of possessive way in which he talked about freedom, does not impress me very much. He was good enough to say when he left the chamber that he would be back when I was speaking. I do not blame him for not coming back; I just regret having to say this in his absence.
The southern racists in the United States believe that freedom gives them the right to have white children educated in one school and black children educated in another school. That is their definition of freedom. If the law did not intervene, they would exercise that "freedom" and continue to segregate the white from the black.
Take the case of the landlord in Ontario who says of his property: "My freedom in this society gives me the right to decide whether or not I am going to rent my property to one person or another. I do not intend to rent it to a Jew or to a Negro. If you pass a law which forces me to rent it to a Jew or to a Negro, you are interfering with my freedom", says this dark ages landlord.
The right hon. gentleman spoke a great deal about freedom and then patted himself on the back for wanting to keep Jerry Rubin out of Canada because he wished to come to this country to make speeches of which the right hon. member disapproves. The history of society is full of definitions of freedom, and they are used to serve whatever purpose people in society want them to serve. Appeals to freedom are as numerous, and frequently are as spurious, as quotations from the scripture that are used to satisfy and justify all kinds of acts.
April 9, 1970

What we are discussing here is not the question of freedom in any meaningful sense of the word. I have never known a piece of legislation that has been so misrepresented across the country as has this piece of legislation. I do not often get home early enough to listen to the program "Viewpoint" after the eleven o'clock television news, but I did happen to watch it last night. I heard an editor of the Globe and Mail, a man I do not know but who I am sure is a fine Canadian, and who I am told was, before he became an editor, a member of the cloth, I think a minister of the United Church of Canada.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Don't hold that against him.

I don't hold anything against him except what he said. That gentleman, with the smug omniscience that a combination of minister and editorial writer makes possible said to the people of Canada: "You know, Pierre Burton is saying bad things about the members of Jehovah's Witnesses who will not permit their children to have blood transfusions. He can do that now with impunity, but one month from now he will be in jail if he says this".
I say to this editorial writer for the Globe and Mail that he does not know what he is talking about. He has not read the bill. He is indulging in hyperbole, in distortion, in misrepresentation, and he is not serving the people of Canada in any sense of the word. What kind of nonsense is this! Where in this bill is there this kind of prohibition?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
It
provides the very opposite.

The bill provides, first of all, that in order to be convicted or to stand a chance of being convicted under the terms of this bill the Crown has to prove that the statements complained of are made in public; that they are calculated to promote hatred of an identifiable group; that the intention of the person making the statements is to promote and evoke hatred of an identifiable group, a minority in our society.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Then, it provides the defence that any decent discussion on a religious subject is a defence against any charge under this bill. So, there is no such possibility of Pierre Berton being in trouble for saying this, at least. I do not know what else Pierre may be in trouble about, but at least in this case he has nothing to worry about.
Hate Propaganda
The same thing has happened in this House. It is easy to say this is terrible legislation and it will prevent this and that, but the fact is that these statements are incorrect, they are not true. They make a mockery of plain English when they are presented to this House and the people of Canada.
The right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert indulges in his usual attractive hyperbole when he reminds this House that a similar law was passed by the U.S.S.R. in 1919, I do not know, maybe it was; I have not the slightest notion. However, he does not tell this House what every member who has read the special report on hate propaganda knows now, that this law was passed by the United Kingdom, by Norway, Sweden, Denmark, France and Switzerland, indeed by every democracy in Europe which does not take second place to the democratic declarations of the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert or to the democratic declarations of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or anyone else in this House or in this country. Is it suggested that the people in all these countries in western Europe have not got as much regard for freedom and democratic rights as we have? What really is the sense and the purpose of a leading member of the Canadian community and in this House trying to besmirch and smear this legislation by reference to some law in a Communist country in 1919? What is the purpose of it, Mr. Speaker? Is that the way this kind of debate should be carried on? Is that the way to place this matter before the House and the people of Canada?
I have in my hand a copy of the relevant sections of the Race Relations Act of 1965 of the United Kingdom passed by the House of Commons, if my memory serves me correctly, with the approval and support in principle of the Conservative opposition at the time as well as the Labour government, and passed by the House of Lords which still has a majority, or at least a very large number of Conservatives in it. It reads:
A person shall be guilty of an offence under this section if, with intent to stir up hatred against any section of the public in Great Britain distinguished by colour, race, or ethnic or national origins-*
(a)	he publishes or distributes written matter which is threatening, abusive or insulting: or
(b)	he uses in any public place or at any public meeting words which are threatening, abusive or insulting, being matter or words likely to stir up hatred against that section on grounds of colour, race, or ethnic or national origins.
In substance this is precisely the kind of legislation that is now before this House,

April 9, 1970
Hate Propaganda
passed by the mother of parliaments to which the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert pays the greatest respect and attention, headed by the monarch to whom the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert pays the homage which the monarch obviously deserves. This is the parliament that passed the kind of legislation which is now before the House, and I think it is a little less than fair and a little less than the fairness of which the right hon. gentleman is usually capable to refer to this legislation as being compared with legislation in the Soviet Union. The fact is, as I have said, all other democratic countries in western Europe have passed similar legislation.
What is this bill all about, Mr. Speaker? Perhaps we ought to spend a minute on that in view of some of the statements I have heard-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Or read.

-or read. What is this bill about? It prohibits the spread, or the advocacy or promotion of genocide. I do not expect that section of this bill will ever have to be used in Canada although, as I shall say in a moment, one can never be certain. But, we undertook an international obligation to put this kind of thing into legislation. As a country we solemnly signed and ratified an international convention on genocide passed by the United Nations, and undertook in that convention to pass this kind of legislation. This section is no more than the fulfilment of our international obligations.
As I said the other day on another subject, the cynical disregard for international obligations is the curse of humanity today, and if we take one small mincing step in fulfilling an obligation under an international convention, then I cannot understand any member of this House questioning this.
The second offence is, and forgive me for reading some of the actual words, because they have been so misrepresented:
Every one who, by communicating statements in any public place, incites hatred against any identifiable group where such incitement is likely to lead to a breach of the peace, is guilty of-
Is anyone suggesting that it is improper to put into the Criminal Code a prohibition against the incitement of hatred that leads to a breach of the peace? Is there anyone here who suggests that there is something wrong in that or that there is an interference with freedom of speech when the Parliament of Canada prohibits this kind of behaviour?

If you will permit me as a lawyer, Mr. Speaker, let me indicate to you how false have been the editorials in certain papers and some of the speeches in trying to interpret this. A prosecuting attorney on a charge under this section will not have an easy time. He has to prove first that the statement was communicated in a public place, that the statement incited hatred and that the statement incited such hatred that is likely to lead to a breach of the peace. There are safeguards right in there, I suggest to you. That is not an interference with freedom in any meaningful sense. That is a provision and a necessary addition to the Criminal Code.
I think perhaps at this point I should call it five o'clock. I will have to continue in the evening.
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Mr. Philip G. Givens (York West) moved
speechtext:
that Bill S-18, respecting Brunner Corporation (Canada) Limited, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills and Standing Orders.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in addressing myself to the second reading of this bill, I want to make it amply clear to the House that I am not connected with this company either directly or indirectly as an officer or shareholder. My name is attached to this bill simply because I was visited by the president and another official of the company which has a branch plant in my constituency. They asked me to be the sponsor of this bill as a result of representations they made to me.
I do not know how much detail hon. members of the House would like me to go into on this subject, but the sole purpose of the bill is to revive the charter of the company. What happened was that during the period between August 8, 1956 and June 6, 1968 there was a comptroller or official of this company whose responsibility it was to make the annual returns, including tax returns, for the compa-
April 9, 1970

Labour Conditions
ny. He had a psychological block about bureaucracy and governmental returns. He just did not make them. Even though there were reminders from the government under Section 125 of the Canada Corporations Act, he failed to make the returns and as a result the charter lapsed. Therefore, the company was placed in this very invidious position.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
The purpose of this bill is merely to restore the charter to the company, so that the company may be returned to the position it was in prior to the difficulty in respect of the filing of these returns. The tax obligations and liabilities of this company would remain as before. There are no privileges to be granted to the company. The company could make application for a new charter, but the difficulty and expense involved in doing so would probably result, in so far as the branch plant in my constituency is concerned, in the company going out of business. I, therefore, pray that the House entertain this bill and pass it for the reasons I have indicated.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.
Could the hon. member tell us whether the comptroller has been fired or whether the company has the same comptroller.
He has become as functus as the charter. He is no longer with the company.

Mr. Speaker, this is another example of the type of bill which I think the government is very foolish in pushing to this level. I accept the explanation given because it sounds illogically logical and, of course, the company would have been put to a great deal of expense to obtain a new charter. I have been involved in considerable discussion in respect of other bills concerning companies which were placed in this position. It was my understanding that the department would take a look at the situation to determine whether the companies involved were interested in maintaining their charter. Such action would make this type of operation unnecessary. There is an expenditure involved here of a considerable amount of money. I do not think this should be necessary. I think the companies branch should have to give a good explanation, because this would seem to be an exercise in futility.
As I remember the last such episode, the instructions given to the branch were that the company would be contacted to determine whether or not it wished to retain its charter. If the company did wish to retain its charter, then a penalty or whatever action was necessary could be applied. In this way the situation could be handled through the normal administrative procedures necessary for reinstatement. It seems to me that by following the procedure we have here we are putting many people, including the hon. member for York West (Mr. Givens) in a difficult position. The hon. member has already pointed out the position in which he has been put.
In my opinion, when this bill is discussed before the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills and Standing Orders, the officials of the department should be asked to give a pretty good reason for having taken this particular step. I do not believe this procedure is a desirable one. I would think that there should be an alternative administrative procedure which should be adhered to by officials of the department.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills and Standing Orders.

The department is now concluding a departmental review of the minimum wage and its effect on the

Canadian economy and, particularly, its effect on programs financed jointly by the provinces and the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, in this age of participatory democracy, Information Canada, public involvement in the decision-making process and all these other things, it seems to me it is a most reasonable request for us to ask that this review, which the Department of Labour has made, be made public. Obviously this is not a document which sets out a policy or any secrets the government may have. We are told it is a review of the minimum wage and the effect of the minimum wage on the Canadian economy. Frankly, we would be much happier if instead of having a review, a white paper, or a document of this kind, we could have a bill amending the appropriate legislation, but as these things take time I ask why we should not be taken into the confidence of the government concerning what it has learned in this study.
Only today during the question period the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took some credit for the government's policy of issuing a white paper on taxation. [DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
If that is the motto of this government, why not practice it? point. AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton) for the third reading of Bill C-3, to amend the Criminal Code.

Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock I was dealing with some of the clauses of the bill in an attempt to point out that the purport and effect of the bill, no doubt in good faith, have been widely misrepresented outside the House and to some extent, in my opinion, by some hon. members in the House. I had finished dealing with the second offence created in the bill, and now I want to say a word about the third offence and ask hon. members who feel uneasy about the bill whether their uneasiness is really justified.
In effect this measure prohibits public communication of statements which wilfully promote hatred against any identifiable group. I wish hon. members and some editorial writers would read the pertinent clause and not precisely what it says. First, it excludes any private conversation. Second, it prohibits the communication of statements which wilfully promote hatred. No matter how you define the word "wilful" in a particular situation,
Hate Propaganda
obviously what this bill says in simple English is that anyone who sets out to make statements deliberately intended to promote hatred against a race, or a group identified by racial or religious aspects, is committing an offence. It is not, therefore, saying something about Jehovah's Witnesses being wrong in not permitting their children to take blood transfusions. It is not any interference with anything that I or anyone else may want to say about Jews, Negroes, Catholics or Protestants.
In order to come within the ambit of this clause I have to say something dirty or scurrilous, and not merely say something dirty or scurrilous but say it with the intention of promoting hatred-say it in such a way, in such circumstances and in such a context that the court can find I deliberately intended to promote hatred against the identifiable group.
I ask hon. members, where is that an interference with my legitimate freedom?
As I said earlier, I listened with great interest to the speech made this afternoon by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). I do not have his exact words, but I agree with him when he says freedom is the right to say something of which the majority may disapprove and with which the majority may disagree. Of course that is what freedom means. I do not believe it should be a schoolbook for those needing primary courses in conduct. We are supposed to learn these things in other ways.
I realize my time is limited, Mr. Speaker, and I should like to conclude by making one or two quotations which illustrate the concern felt in this issue by hon. members, especially on this side of the House. In the words of Justice Holmes, if there was a clear and present danger presented by the ills which this bill is supposed to cure, there might be justification for approving the proposals put forward by the government. I do not think there is such a danger. The bill is negative in quality. It will have a chilling effect not only on the occasional oddball who may be prosecuted but on many other persons who may from now on be afraid to speak out lest they become liable to the penalties set out.
I conclude by quoting the words of Mr. Justice Jackson in the case of American Communications Association v. Dodds, 339 U.S., 382, as recorded at page 442. Justice Jackson said, among other things:
The danger that citizens will think wrongly is serious, hut less serious than the danger of atrophy through not thinking-

I thank the House for its qualified approval. It is only because I was in the middle of my concluding quotation that the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney), who was not even listening-I do not blame him for that-said no. Mr. Justice Jackson, among other things, said:
It is not the function of the government to keep the citizens from falling into error. It is the function of the citizens to keep the government from falling into error.
Every time the House passes a negative, repressive piece of legislation which restricts the full expression of opinion, even though the opinions expressed may be odious, we fall into error and a lever is removed by means of which bad government could be corrected.

Perhaps I can make one point before Your Honour sees it is ten o'clock. I would say on behalf of my hon. friends that the vote this afternoon on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Wool-liams) is an accurate reflection of our attitude regarding the disposition of this measure as a whole. I say this in order that our views may be identified on such an important issue.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Because your hon. friends refused me permission to do so earlier. Tomorrow, as hon. members know, will be an allotted today, the subject matter being chosen by the New Democratic Party. On Monday we would call as the first item third reading of Bill C-3 currently under consideration, and would hope to follow shortly thereafter with second reading of the Canada grain bill. It is anticipated this will be a popular subject matter and we therefore expect to spend some part of Tuesday on its discussion. On Wednesday the budget debate will be continued for the fifth appointed day, and on Thursday we shall consider Government Order No. 87, Bill C-202 in connection with measures against pollution in the Arctic seas.
At 10 p.m. the House adjourned, without question put, pursuant to Standing Order.
